extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of Euclidean geometry (undergraduate/advanced-secondary level)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of classical Euclidean construction problems, definitions, and theorems (Book IV) covering constructions with straightedge and compass: inscribing/describing circles and regular polygons, centres of triangles, and related metric relations; followed by introductory definitions for the Theory of Proportion (Book V).

rubrics_metrics.name: To inscribe a circle in a given triangle (Prop. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect any two angles A, B of the given triangle by the lines AO, BO; then O, their point of intersection, is the centre of the required circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: From O drop perpendiculars OD, OE, OF to the sides; show OE = OF and OD = OF so all perpendicular distances from O to sides are equal. The circle with centre O and radius OD passes through the feet and, since the angles at the feet are right, touches the three sides. Exercises and corollaries follow (concurrency of bisectors, distances from vertices to contact points, escribed circles, relations involving r, r', s, area, Heron's formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal angle bisectors of the three angles of a triangle meet at a single point (the incenter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from construction for inscribing a circle; exercise points to compare with other propositions (I.xxvi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distances from vertices to points of contact of inscribed circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If sides BC, CA, AB are denoted by a, b, c and half their sum by s, the distances of vertices A, B, C from the points of contact of the inscribed circle are respectively s−a, s−b, s−c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as Exercise 2 following Prop. IV; used in metric relations with inradius and area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escribed (exscribed) circles construction and centres
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect the external angles of the triangle; the angular points O', O'', O''' of the triangle formed by the three bisectors are the centres of three circles, each touching one side externally and the other two produced (escribed circles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises give distances from vertices to points of contact for escribed circles (s, s−a, etc.), and concurrency / cyclic relations among incenter and excentres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations between inradius, exradius, semiperimeter and area
rubrics_metrics.description: If r is radius of inscribed circle and s semiperimeter, then r s = area of the triangle. If r' is radius of the exscribed circle touching side a externally, then r'(s−a) = area of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also listed: rr' = (s−b)(s−c) (stated as Exercise 11), and Heron's formula: (area)^2 = s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c) (Exercise 12). Additional relations include product of radii of in- and ex-circles (Exercise 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: To describe a circle about a given triangle (circumcircle) (Prop. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect any two sides BC, AC in points D, E. Erect DO, EO at right angles to BC, CA; their intersection O is the circumcentre; the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through A, B, C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: perpendicular bisectors meet at a point equidistant from vertices. Corollary: perpendiculars at middle points of sides are concurrent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: circumcircle, circumradius, circumcentre
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle through A, B, C is the circumcircle of the triangle; its radius is the circumradius and its centre is the circumcentre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to derive properties about perpendiculars, orthocentre, and nine-point circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three perpendiculars from vertices to opposite sides are concurrent (orthocentre) (Exercise/Prop.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perpendiculars from the vertices of a triangle to the opposite sides meet at a common point O, called the orthocentre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via circumscribed circle and symmetry arguments; alternative short proof given using parallels and a larger triangle described about ABC. Subsequent definitions and properties of orthocentre follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar circle and its defining product relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle about O as centre whose radius squared equals the common product OA·OP = OB·OQ = OC·OR is called the polar circle of triangle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: when the orthocentre lies inside the triangle these directed products are negative and the polar circle is imaginary; it's real when the orthocentre is outside (obtuse triangle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nine-point circle (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nine points made up of the feet of the perpendiculars, the midpoints of the sides, and the midpoints of the segments from the vertices to the orthocentre are concyclic; the circle through these is the nine-points circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: the radius of the nine-points circle equals half the circumradius; its centre has equal distance (the radius) to those nine points; its relation to circumcircle and triangles formed by in- and ex-centres are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance relations involving orthocentre and circumcentre
rubrics_metrics.description: The distances between the vertices of a triangle and its orthocentre are respectively twice the perpendiculars from the circumcentre on the sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among corollaries/exercises following Prop. V; used to derive nine-point and other metric properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: In a circle, to inscribe a square (Prop. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw two diameters at right angles AC, BD; join AB, BC, CD, DA to form square ABCD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses equality of arcs subtended by right angles at centre and right angles subtended by diameters giving right angles at vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: About a given circle to describe a square (Prop. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw two perpendicular diameters and at the four points draw tangents to the circle; the quadrilateral formed by consecutive tangents is a square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by showing tangent directions are parallel to radii and equalities produce lozenge shapes that are squares; corollary: circumscribed square area is double inscribed square area.

rubrics_metrics.name: In a given square to inscribe a circle (Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect two adjacent sides; through the bisection points draw parallels to the opposite sides; their intersection O is the centre of the inscribed circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AO equals half the side, so OA = OB = OC = OD, and circle with centre O and that radius is inscribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: About a given square to describe a circle (Prop. IX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw diagonals AC, BD; their intersection O is the centre of the required circumscribed circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangles formed by diagonal halves are isosceles/right so OA = OB = OC = OD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of an isosceles triangle with base angles double the vertical angle (Prop. X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given base AB, find point C on AB so that rectangle AB·BC = AC^2; with A centre and AB radius draw circle BDE and set chord BD = AC; triangle ABD has each base angle double the vertical angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses circle tangency and angle-chasing; exercises explore connections to regular pentagon and decagon constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: To inscribe a regular pentagon in a given circle (Prop. XI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an isosceles triangle with each base angle double the vertical angle; inscribe an equiangular triangle ABD in the given circle equiangular to it; bisect angles DAB and ABD to locate remaining vertices C,E and form regular pentagon ABCDE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof that chords and arcs so obtained are equal; exercises include properties of diagonals, relationships to pentagon/decagon side lengths and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: To describe a regular pentagon about a given circle (Prop. XII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a regular inscribed pentagon ABCDE, draw tangents at A,B,C,D,E; the polygon formed by consecutive tangents FGHIJ is a circumscribed regular pentagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses equal central angles and tangent-right-angle properties; general theorem: tangents at vertices of any inscribed regular polygon form a circumscribed regular polygon of same number of sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: To inscribe a circle in a regular pentagon (Prop. XIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect two adjacent angles A, B by AO, BO; their intersection O is centre of inscribed circle which has equal perpendiculars to all five sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof shows perpendicular distances from O to sides are equal using congruent right triangles; same method applies to any regular polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: To describe a circle about a regular pentagon (Prop. XIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect two adjacent angles A, B; their intersection O is the circumcentre; OA = OB = OC = OD = OE so the circle with centre O passes through all pentagon vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same method extends to any regular polygon: regular polygon has one inscribed and one circumscribed circle, concentric.

rubrics_metrics.name: To inscribe a regular hexagon in a given circle (Prop. XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take any point A; with centre A and radius AO mark off consecutive points around circle to obtain vertices B,C,D,E,F so ABCDEF is regular hexagon (each central angle = 60°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries: side of inscribed regular hexagon equals the radius; three alternate vertices form an equilateral triangle. Exercises compare areas with equilateral triangles and circumscribed hexagons.

rubrics_metrics.name: To inscribe a regular 15-gon in a given circle (Prop. XVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe a regular pentagon and an equilateral triangle in the circle; join appropriate vertices (difference of arcs) to obtain a side GC and replicate around to get a regular 15-gon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration uses arc arithmetic: arc GC equals (1/5 − 1/3) of circumference = 1/15. Scholium: historical note on constructible regular polygons; Gauss result for special primes mentioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: General theorem: tangents at vertices of an inscribed regular polygon form circumscribed regular polygon
rubrics_metrics.description: If tangents are drawn to a circle at the angular points of an inscribed polygon of any number of sides, they will form a regular polygon of the same number of sides circumscribed to the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given as a generalisation of Proposition XII; used to create circumscribed regular polygons from inscribed ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular polygon concentric inscribed and circumscribed circles
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular polygon of any number of sides has one circle inscribed in it and another described about it, and both circles are concentric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions XIII and XIV are particular cases; proof pattern generalises to any regular polygon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific metric and combinatorial exercises and identities (selected)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of exercises and identities: e.g., side of regular hexagon equals radius; area relations between inscribed/circumscribed polygons; many loci and concurrency results; relations among radii R, r, r', r'', δ, μ with stated sums (r' + r'' + r''' = 4R + r; μ + μ' + μ'' = 2R − r; δ + δ' + δ'' = R + r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises collect numerous theorems to be proved from the preceding propositions; many are metric identities tying inradius, circumradius, exradii, semiperimeter and areas (Heron's formula etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on constructible regular polygons (historical note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 1801 only certain regular polygons could be constructed by straightedge and compass; in 1801 Gauss proved that if 2^n + 1 is a prime number, regular polygons of 2^n + 1 sides are inscriptable by elementary geometry (text notes n=4 case as special).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context; points to deeper number-theoretic criterion for constructibility (Gauss' theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions for Theory of Proportion (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: (i) a less magnitude is a part/submultiple of a greater when it measures the greater; (ii) a greater magnitude is a multiple of a less when it is measured by the less; (iii) ratio is the mutual relation of two magnitudes of the same kind with respect to quantity; (iv) magnitudes have a ratio when the less can be multiplied so as to exceed the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes Def. (iii) is obscure historically and proceeds to explain via fractions, numerators/denominators, operations on fractions, conversion between ratios and fractions for commensurable magnitudes, and approximation (convergents) for incommensurable ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional notation and invariance under scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: A fraction is two numbers with numerator and denominator; multiplying numerator and denominator by same whole number does not change value, likewise dividing both by same whole number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with line AB divided into equal parts; fundamental theorem: multiply or divide both terms by any whole number without changing fraction value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of ratios to fractions and convergents for incommensurables
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of two commensurable magnitudes equals the ratio of the numbers expressing their measures and can be converted to a fraction; for incommensurable quantities a sequence of convergent fraction pairs approximates the ratio arbitrarily closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to approach irrational ratios (e.g., diagonal to side of square) by convergents; sets up algebraic viewpoint for Book V.
